anchor: Careful observers may foretell the hour
title: Occasion and publication
short: Written in October 1710 and printed in Steele's Tatler No. 238 (17 Oct. 1710); Swift reported it was thought 'the best thing I ever writ'.
body: Swift wrote the poem during his London stay of autumn 1710; his letters to Esther Johnson ('Stella') follow its progress and on 17 October report that the Tatler had come out 'made up wholly of my Shower' and that people said it was the best thing he ever wrote, and he thought so too. On 27 October he reports that Rowe and Prior said there never was such a shower since Danae's. It is a companion to his 'Description of the Morning' (Tatler No. 9, 1709). Both apply the precise, low, urban detail of satire to genres of elevated description, producing a mock-georgic or 'town eclogue'. It was reprinted in Swift's Miscellanies of 1711, and later printings differ in details of wording.

title: sure prognostics
short: Weather signs: a parody of Virgil's Georgics 1, which lists the 'sure signs' of coming rain and storms.
body: Virgil's Georgics 1.351-92 opens a catalogue of weather signs with the claim that we may learn them by sure signs ('certis ... signis'), drawn from Aratus's Phaenomena; signs include animals' behaviour such as cattle sniffing the air and frogs croaking. Swift translates the didactic catalogue to London: the cat, the sink, corns and aching teeth are the city's signs. Brendan O Hehir's influential essay read the whole poem as a sustained parody of Virgil's Georgics, and of Dryden's 1697 translation, with an apocalyptic undertone of the Flood.

title: depends
short: A Latinism: 'hangs overhead, is impending' (Latin dependere, 'hang down').
body: Swift uses the word in its root sense, the rain hanging in the clouds before it falls; the elevated Latinism contrasts comically with the 'pensive cat', whose frolics and tail-chasing stop as a sign of rain. Cats' behaviour was part of popular weather lore, a domestic substitute for Virgil's birds and cattle. Swift's verb 'gives o'er' and the cat's 'frolics' keep a mock-dignified tone, as if the cat were a melancholy philosopher abandoning her pleasures.

title: the sink
short: A cesspool or drain; its smell grows worse before rain. Swift had his own lodging's sink in mind.
body: A sink was a pit or drain for foul water and sewage. Lowering air pressure before rain was observed to release the stink. In a letter to Stella of 31 October 1710 (Letter 8) Swift complained that he was almost stunk out of his lodging by the sink, adding that it helped him to verses in his 'Shower'. 'Double stink' and the following coach-hire couplet (go not far to dine, or you will pay more for a coach home than you save on wine) give the Georgics' practical advice an urban, economical twist.

title: a-ches
short: 'Aches' pronounced as two syllables ('aitches'), the older form; the hyphen preserves the metre.
body: The noun 'ache' was formerly pronounced like the letter H, with the plural 'aches' in two syllables, as in Shakespeare's Tempest 1.2 ('Fill all thy bones with aches'). Swift's spelling 'a-ches' marks the pronunciation. Some later printings read 'Old aches will throb', which treats the word as one syllable and pads the line with 'will'. Shooting corns and a hollow tooth are bodily barometers.

title: Dulman and the spleen
short: A type-name ('dull man') for an idle coffee-house lounger who blames the weather for his 'spleen', the fashionable melancholy.
body: Swift's invented name labels a type, in the manner of the Tatler and Spectator's character sketches. 'Spleen' was the fashionable name for low spirits, hypochondria and ill-humour, a melancholy thought especially English and blamed on the damp climate. Coffee-houses were the centres of London news and idleness. The sauntering Dulman is the poem's first human weather-sign: like the cat and the aching tooth, his complaint signals rain. His damning of the climate is the typical grumble of the idle: talk in place of Virgil's useful labour.

anchor: the South, rising with dabbled wings
title: the South, rising with dabbled wings
short: The south wind, bringer of rain, with wet wings, a mock-heroic echo of Ovid's Notus before the Flood.
body: In Ovid's account of the Flood (Metamorphoses 1.264), Jupiter releases the south wind Notus, who flies out 'madidis ... alis', with soaking wings, and pours down rain. Swift's 'dabbled' (splashed, soiled with wet) brings the classical deity down to street level. The cloud that 'swill'd more liquor than it could contain' and 'gives it up again' like a drunkard turns the sublime storm into a London tavern image of vomiting.

title: athwart the welkin
short: Poetic diction: 'across the sky'. 'Welkin' (Old English wolcen, cloud) was already archaic and 'poetical'.
body: Swift deliberately uses the stock vocabulary of elevated verse, 'sable' for black, 'athwart' for across, 'welkin' for sky, to describe a London rain cloud. The mismatch between diction and subject is the engine of the mock-georgic. Pope ridiculed similar poetic diction in Peri Bathous (1728). 'Flings' gives the cloud a sudden, violent movement, and 'sable' (heraldic black) dignifies what is merely a dark rain cloud over the city.

title: Brisk Susan ... careless quean
short: A 'quean' is a hussy or slattern, a coarse word for a servant girl; her mop flicks dirty water at passers-by.
body: 'Brisk Susan' is a generic servant name. 'Aslope' means slanting, aslant. The 'quean' (from Old English cwene, woman, which came to mean a low or impudent woman) 'flirts' (flicks) water from her mop, a sprinkling like the first rain 'but not so clean'. The victim flies, 'invokes the gods' in epic fashion, then stops to swear at her while she goes on singing. The mock-epic invocation is reduced to cursing a maid.

title: the battle of dust and rain
short: A mock-epic battle between dust and rain, parodying a line in Garth's The Dispensary about sea and sky.
body: The dust 'fought still for life' in an 'unequal strife', aided by its ally the wind, epic battle language. The last line echoes a line in Samuel Garth's mock-heroic The Dispensary (1699) about sea and sky, to which a note in the 1735 Works draws attention. Garth's line in turn recalls descriptions of the Flood (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.292: all was sea, and the sea had no shores). Swift's parody of a parody multiplies the literary layers.

sources.cite: Samuel Garth, The Dispensary (1699)

title: needy poet ... Sole coat!
short: The poor poet's only coat is ruined by dust cemented with rain; a mock-heroic apostrophe in the manner of epic lament.
body: 'Ah! where must needy poet seek for aid' parodies the epic or tragic apostrophe. The joke is the hack writer's poverty, a constant theme of Augustan satire (compare Swift's own Grub Street pieces and Pope's Dunciad). Rain 'erects the nap' (raises the short fibres of the cloth) and leaves a stain. The 1711 Miscellanies text reads 'His only Coat, where Dust confus'd with Rain'; the sharper 'Sole coat!' and 'cemented' belong to a later revision.

sources.cite: Harold Williams, ed., The Poems of Jonathan Swift, 2nd edn (1958), vol. 1, notes to 'A Description of a City Shower'

title: deluge ... this devoted town
short: 'Devoted' in its Latin sense, 'doomed, consigned to destruction'; the shower becomes a mock Flood on sinful London.
body: Latin devotus means vowed to the gods, hence doomed. The 'contiguous drops' (touching, continuous) make a 'flood' that threatens 'deluge', inviting comparison with God's punishment of a corrupt world in Genesis 6-7 and with Ovid's flood (Metamorphoses 1.253-312), and with the destruction of Troy. O Hehir argued that the poem's final flood of filth enacts a mock Last Judgement on the city, while other critics think the apocalyptic reading overstated.

title: daggled females ... cheapen goods
short: Mud-splashed women take shelter in shops, pretending to haggle over goods they have no intention of buying.
body: 'Daggled' means splashed and soiled with mud, of skirts trailing in wet streets. To 'cheapen' was to ask the price of, bargain for (from Old English ceap, trade). The couplet captures a social comedy: the rain turns shops into shelters and customers into pretenders. Throughout this section Swift catalogues social types (women shoppers, a Templar, a sempstress, party men, a beau), each revealed by how they behave in the rain.

title: The Templar spruce
short: A smart young law student of the Inner or Middle Temple, who lingers in shelter while pretending to hail a coach.
body: Templars were members of the Inns of Court at the Temple, often fashionable young men more interested in town pleasures than law. 'Spruce' means neat, dapper. 'Abroach' means pouring out, as of a cask that has been tapped: every rain-spout is running. He 'seems to call a coach' to save face but will not pay for one, matching the earlier coach-hire economy (l. 8).

title: oil'd umbrella
short: Umbrellas of oiled cloth or silk were then used mainly by women; the 'tuck'd-up sempstress' has her skirts pinned up out of the mud.
body: In the early eighteenth century the umbrella was chiefly a woman's accessory; men who carried one could be mocked as effeminate, and Gay's Trivia (1716) also treats it as a female item. The waterproofing was done with oil. A sempstress, a seamstress, is a working woman who cannot afford to wait or ride; 'tuck'd-up' means her skirts are pinned up out of the wet. Her purposeful stride contrasts with the Templar's affected idleness in the couplet before.

title: Triumphant Tories, and desponding Whigs
short: Topical: in autumn 1710 the Whig ministry fell and the Tories under Harley won the October general election; Swift was changing sides.
body: Queen Anne dismissed the Whig Godolphin ministry in August 1710, and the Tories won a sweeping victory in the elections of October, just as the poem appeared. Swift, a Whig by origin, was then being courted by Robert Harley and would soon become the chief Tory propagandist, as the Journal to Stella records. The joke is that party feuds yield to the common need to save expensive periwigs from the rain under a shed.

title: The beau in his chair and the Trojan horse
short: A mock-epic simile: the beau trapped in a sedan chair drummed by rain is like the Greeks inside the wooden horse when Laocoon struck it with his spear.
body: A 'chair' is a sedan chair carried by two chairmen; its leather roof 'sounds' under the rain. In Aeneid 2.50-53 Laocoon hurls his spear into the side of the wooden horse, and the hollow belly echoes; Virgil's Greeks, Swift implies, quaked inside. Swift adds a contemporary joke: 'bully Greeks', like modern rakes, ran their chairmen through instead of paying them. The simile is a full epic simile in form, applied to a fop.

title: kennels
short: Street gutters (from 'channel'), which carry the city's refuse along as rivers bear spoils or 'trophies'.
body: 'Kennel' is a variant of 'channel': the open gutter running down the middle or side of a street. The gutters 'bear their trophies' like a victorious army carrying spoils, a mock-heroic image; the filth reveals 'What street they sail'd from, by their sight and smell', so that refuse becomes a guide to London's trades. The verb 'sail'd' continues the mock-heroic voyage; Swift treats the gutters as epic rivers flowing to their confluence.

title: Smithfield, St Pulchre's, Snowhill, Holborn bridge
short: The flood runs downhill from Smithfield meat market past St Sepulchre's church and Snow Hill into the Fleet Ditch at Holborn Bridge.
body: Smithfield was London's livestock market, notorious for blood and offal. 'St. Pulchre's' is the colloquial name of St Sepulchre-without-Newgate. Snow Hill ran steeply down to Holborn Bridge, which crossed the Fleet Ditch, an open sewer famous for filth; the 'conduit' was a water conduit on Snow Hill. Pope later set the diving contest of The Dunciad (1728) in the Fleet Ditch. The route traces an actual drainage path, giving the mock-epic river a real geography.

sources.cite: Pat Rogers, ed., Jonathan Swift: The Complete Poems (Penguin, 1983), notes ad loc.

title: The closing triplet and Alexandrine
short: The poem ends with three rhyming lines, the last a twelve-syllable Alexandrine, parodying a mannerism of Dryden and his imitators.
body: Dryden often closed a verse paragraph with a triplet (three rhymes) ending in an Alexandrine (a twelve-syllable line); in the dedication of his Aeneis (1697) he defended both licences. Editors since the eighteenth century have read Swift's final triplet and Alexandrine as a jibe at this habit. Swift heaps 'dung, guts, and blood, / Drown'd puppies, stinking sprats' and 'Dead cats' into the stately form, so the swollen line tumbles like the flood itself.
